clue.text: Film with endless sex due for distribution having received approval

indicators.note: a word with no end has given up its final letter, so the piece named arrives one short
what is put out for distribution is handed round in no set order, and these letters go the same way
what you receive you take in, so the piece named next lands inside the shuffled letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters, the connective taken as letters
the three letters of SEX with the last one deleted, which is what 'endless' asks for
anagram fodder, three letters
approval spoken out loud is a yes

explanation.surface: A film whose non-stop sex scenes were due for release once the censor had finally signed it off.
explanation.walkthrough: Kubrick's last film, delivered days before he died in 1999. 'With' and 'due' read as the sentence's grammar and are seven of the letters being shuffled, which is what makes the fodder so hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Film -> EYES WIDE SHUT: Stanley Kubrick's 1999 feature with Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman, one title standing in for the general word.

clue.text: French article supports being less variable in style

indicators.note: down the column, whatever supports the rest holds it up from underneath, so this piece takes the bottom squares
less something is that something subtracted, so the letter named after it goes

blocks.note: a being is an ENTITY, which here gives up the letter named next
x and y are the variables of school algebra, and this is the one coming off the end
le is the masculine 'the' in French

explanation.surface: A point of French grammar propping up the idea that a steadier way of writing is the better one.
explanation.walkthrough: Y is algebra's variable, so 'less variable' is a subtraction rather than praise for consistency. To entitle is to style: a book entitled Bleak House is a book styled that.
explanation.definitionFit: style -> ENTITLE: both verbs mean to give a thing its name, as a work styled or entitled such-and-such.

clue.text: Serious composer imprisoned in Estonia

indicators.note: a prisoner is shut up inside the walls, so this piece sits within the letters named next

blocks.note: EST is Estonia's international code, on its cars and its web addresses
Thomas Arne wrote 'Rule, Britannia!' and is the composer setters reach for when four letters are wanted

explanation.surface: A grave-faced composer locked up somewhere in the Baltic.
explanation.walkthrough: Arne, an eighteenth-century Londoner, is worth learning: his name turns up whenever a composer is wanted short. Wilde's play is the other place this word gets to be a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Serious -> EARNEST: both describe someone in deadly sincerity, meaning what they say with no joke anywhere in it.

clue.text: A silly place to grow plants?

definitions.text: A silly place to grow plants?

blocks.note: read as a daft spot to choose, and meant as a place on or beside a sill
the only thing such a place is built for: a shallow trough of soil, geraniums in summer and bulbs in spring

explanation.surface: Someone pointing out an absurd spot for gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' is doing the hiding: a sill-y place is a place on a sill, which is where the trough of soil is fixed. The surface reading, a daft choice of garden, is the whole of the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: The trough bolted outside a window is genuinely where a flat with no garden grows things, and 'silly' is the sill it stands on with a letter added.

clue.text: Bash a drug supplier

blocks.note: a bash is a party, and so is a do
sixty miles an hour is sixty miles per hour, so the article swaps straight for the preposition

explanation.surface: An instruction to go and thump the local dealer.
explanation.walkthrough: A doper is the one who administers the drug, to a racehorse or a cyclist, rather than the one who takes it. All the violence in the sentence comes from a word that here means a party.
explanation.definitionFit: drug supplier -> DOPER: the person who dopes an animal or an athlete is the one putting the drug into them.

clue.text: Italian composer unsettled by Israeli

indicators.note: somebody unsettled will not stay put, and neither will the letters described that way

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: An Italian composer thrown off his stride by an Israeli.
explanation.walkthrough: Antonio Salieri was Mozart's rival at the Viennese court, and Peter Shaffer's play Amadeus turned him into his poisoner. He was in fact Vienna's most sought-after teacher, with Beethoven and Schubert among his pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian composer -> SALIERI: Antonio Salieri, born near Verona and court composer in Vienna, one name standing for the general description.

clue.text: What's described by Uyghur ode? Large amphibians

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw it round something, so these words are enclosing the answer rather than building it

blocks.note: seven letters running on unbroken from the end of the first word, through the second and into the third

explanation.surface: Someone asking what a Uyghur poem is about, and being told big amphibians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large' looks like half the definition and is in fact the last of the hiding place. Urodela is the zoological order of tailed amphibians, newts and salamanders among them.
explanation.definitionFit: amphibians -> URODELA: the scientific order covering newts and salamanders, the amphibians that keep their tails into adult life.

clue.text: A cook involved in cooking halal food gets very agitated

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so this piece goes within the letters named next

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
to cook the dinner is to do it, with the article joined on in front

explanation.surface: A chef caught up in preparing halal food and working himself into a state.
explanation.walkthrough: All of a doodah is British for flustered, the same idiom as in a tizzy or all of a dither. 'A cook' is not a person here: it is the article and a verb meaning do.
explanation.definitionFit: very agitated -> ALL OF A DOODAH: the idiom for somebody in a complete flap, worked up well past the point of thinking straight.

clue.text: Not now an official papal residence? It was once

definitions.text: Not now an official papal residence? It was once

blocks.note: what is not happening now happens later
the article joins on exactly as it stands

explanation.surface: A note that a grand building the popes used to live in is no longer their address.
explanation.walkthrough: St John Lateran is still Rome's cathedral and the pope's own church; the palace beside it housed the popes until they left for Avignon and came back to the Vatican instead. Every word here defines as well as builds.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the Lateran was the popes' official residence in Rome for a thousand years and has not been one since the fourteenth century.

clue.text: Stop by the side of the road to pick up old females

definitions.text: Stop by the side of the road

blocks.note: to pull in a pub or a club is to pick somebody up
o. is the short form on any dated label
f is the standard short form for female, doubled because more than one is named

explanation.surface: A driver stopping on the verge to give a couple of older women a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: To pull off is the motorist's move, leaving the carriageway for a lay-by, rather than the 'bring off something difficult' sense a solver reaches for first. Doubling a letter to make it plural is standard practice.
explanation.definitionFit: Stop by the side of the road -> PULL OFF: what a driver does when leaving the carriageway for the verge or a lay-by.

clue.text: Fretful ones touch food items finally

indicators.note: what a word comes to finally is the letter it ends on, and that letter alone

blocks.note: to finger something is to touch it
board is food provided, as in board and lodging
the letter this word ends on, taken as the indicator asks

explanation.surface: Worriers fiddling with the last of the things on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fretful' is the joke: the strip down a guitar or lute neck is the part carrying the frets, so it really is full of them. The surface sense, anxious, has nothing to do with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fretful ones -> FINGERBOARDS: the strips along a guitar or lute neck that hold the frets, full of frets in the literal sense the definition is playing on.

clue.text: Busy pair going round North, say

indicators.note: what goes round a thing closes on it from both sides, so the piece named first sits either side of the letters that follow

blocks.note: a cricketer out for nothing in both innings is given a pair, the two ducks written as a pair of noughts
Nth is the short form of the compass point, as printed on a map
eg is the standard 'for example', which is what 'say' asks for

explanation.surface: A busy couple doing the rounds of somewhere like the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair is the cricketer's: out for nought in both innings, two ducks side by side on the scorecard. 'Busy pair' looks like a single phrase, and only the first word of it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Busy -> ON THE GO: somebody on the go is never still, which is what calling a person busy describes.

clue.text: Heartless theatrical princess keeps dictionary in school

indicators.note: a word with no heart has lost the letter at its very centre
what you keep you hold on to inside, so the piece named next goes within this one

blocks.note: Regan is Lear's second daughter, a princess on the stage, and her middle letter has gone
the Oxford English Dictionary, the one crosswords mean when they say dictionary

explanation.surface: An unfeeling stage princess hoarding a dictionary somewhere in a school.
explanation.walkthrough: Roedean is the girls' boarding school on the cliffs above Brighton. Heartless suits Regan twice over: she is the daughter who helps put out Gloucester's eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: school -> ROEDEAN: the girls' boarding school above Brighton, one particular school standing in for the general word.

clue.text: I spy a toff

definitions.note: The definition speaks in the first person: 'I' stands for the answer itself, so it reads 'I am a spy' rather than being a phrase you could drop into a sentence in place of the word.

blocks.note: the article taken exactly as it stands
British slang for a posh, well-turned-out man; the four letters are the clipped form of gentleman

explanation.surface: Somebody spotting a posh type across the room.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'I' is the answer talking about itself, a device setters use to write a definition in the first person. Toff and gent belong to the same vocabulary of class, which is what makes the swap look like nothing is happening.
explanation.definitionFit: I spy -> AGENT: the answer introduces itself, an agent being someone who spies for a government or a firm.

clue.text: Maybe Ruth will take your family to see Captain Traoré?

definitions.note: The definition names one man instead of giving a synonym: Traoré is a Burkinabe, and the question mark is the setter marking the example.

indicators.note: what somebody takes along they carry inside with them, so the pieces named next sit within the one named first

blocks.note: Babe Ruth, the New York Yankees slugger; 'maybe' flags that one Ruth out of several is wanted
ur is the text-message spelling of the word
your kin are your family

explanation.surface: Ruth might drive the whole family over to meet the captain.
explanation.walkthrough: Ibrahim Traore, an army captain, has run Burkina Faso since seizing power in 2022, and a Burkinabe is anyone from that country. 'Maybe' is what tells you which Ruth: the baseball player, not the biblical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Traoré -> BURKINABE: Traore, the army captain governing Burkina Faso, is himself a Burkinabe, a citizen of that country.

clue.text: God! An idiot's triggered a nuclear hazard

indicators.note: a triggered charge throws everything near it out of place, and these letters land in a new order

blocks.note: Ra is the sun god of ancient Egypt, the deity setters reach for when two letters are wanted
anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: An exclamation of horror at a fool who has set off something nuclear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God!' is an oath in the surface and the Egyptian sun god in the wordplay, which is the one step that has to be seen before the shuffle makes sense. The apostrophe-s is simply 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: a nuclear hazard -> RADIATION: the invisible emission from a reactor or a bomb, the thing that makes either of them dangerous to stand near.

clue.text: Love poetry for adults only – news boss in need of a lot of it

definitions.text: in need of a lot of it

blocks.note: love is the tennis score of nothing, written as a nought
verse is poetry as against prose
the old British film certificate that barred anyone under eighteen
the editor who runs a paper, always shortened

explanation.surface: Adults-only love poetry, and a news editor who cannot get enough of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' has meant sex since the 1920s and the It girl, which is what the definition is leaning on. The X certificate was Britain's adults-only rating until the 18 replaced it in 1982.
explanation.definitionFit: in need of a lot of it -> OVERSEXED: 'it' is the old polite word for sex, and somebody oversexed wants far more of it than is comfortable.

clue.text: Enthusiastic tributes come in a wave

indicators.note: a wave moves everything it passes through, so these letters will not be left standing in their order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters, three little words that look like grammar

explanation.surface: Praise for someone arriving all at once, like a wave breaking.
explanation.walkthrough: An encomium is a formal speech or piece of writing in praise of somebody, from the Greek; encomia is the plural, which is why the definition is plural too.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiastic tributes -> ENCOMIA: encomia are set pieces of high praise, warmer and more formal than a good review.

clue.text: Tot's feet caught in flipping straps

indicators.note: something caught in a thing is stuck inside it, so these letters go within the piece named next
flipped over, a word is read the other way about, its last letter arriving first

blocks.note: the straps a rider holds are REINS, set down here back to front
ft is the short form on any measurement given in them

explanation.surface: A toddler with his feet tangled up in the wretched straps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is the British word for mild exasperation in the surface and an instruction to turn a word round in the wordplay. Reins are the straps setters reach for most.
explanation.definitionFit: Tot -> SNIFTER: both are small measures of spirits, the quick one poured before dinner rather than a full glass.

clue.text: In essence, Le Bon is a star

indicators.note: what is in these words is already sitting there, so the letters are to be found rather than built

blocks.note: five letters running from the tail of the first word straight on through the next two

explanation.surface: A claim that Le Bon is, fundamentally, a star.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Le Bon has fronted Duran Duran since 1980, so the sentence is true as it stands, which is the disguise. 'In essence' reads as an idiom and is half instruction, half hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: a star -> CELEB: a celeb is a famous face, and star is the word the papers use for the same thing.

clue.text: Companion book from France about French parsley

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so this piece is set down in the opposite direction

blocks.note: CH after a name means Companion of Honour, a British order of about sixty living members
a book in France is a livre, written here the other way round

explanation.surface: A friend's French book on the subject of a kitchen herb.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is one thing, not a nationality plus a herb: chervil is the mild aniseed-flavoured leaf in a French fines herbes mix, and British greengrocers sell it as French parsley.
explanation.definitionFit: French parsley -> CHERVIL: the lacy aniseed herb of French cooking, sold under that name here because the leaf looks like flat parsley.

clue.text: Without help, left deeply incapacitated by illness

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, as in a green hill without a city wall: the other pieces stand outside this one

blocks.note: l. is the short form on any set of directions
aid is help
a deep note is a low one, and a deep voice a low voice

explanation.surface: Somebody with nobody to help them, badly floored by sickness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the archaic sense, outside, rather than the everyday 'lacking' the surface wants, and that is what puts help in the middle of the answer rather than out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: incapacitated by illness -> LAID LOW: to be laid low is to be knocked flat by a bug or a fever, off your feet until it lifts.

clue.text: Drop in business after Christmas period

indicators.note: across the grid, what comes after a thing is written to the right of it, so this piece takes the later squares

blocks.note: Dec is December, the month Christmas falls in
the line you are in is your line of business

explanation.surface: Trade falling away once the Christmas rush is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop in business' is the trap: it reads as one phrase, and only the first word of it is the definition. A line is a line of work, as in what line are you in.
explanation.definitionFit: Drop -> DECLINE: both are the noun for a falling-away, whether in takings, in health or in numbers.

clue.text: Memory of online concert

blocks.note: e- is the prefix for anything done online, as in email
a prom is a promenade concert, the summer season the BBC runs at the Albert Hall

explanation.surface: A recollection of a concert watched over the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: An EPROM is erasable programmable read-only memory, the chip you wipe with ultraviolet light and write again. Its last letter stands for the word the definition uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Memory -> EPROM: the chip is one kind of computer memory, an example standing in for the general word.

clue.text: Country girl in pursuit of a male

indicators.note: whoever is in pursuit comes along behind, so this piece is written after the ones it is chasing

blocks.note: the article taken exactly as it stands
m is the box you tick on any form asking
Erica is a girl's name and also the botanical name for heather

explanation.surface: A girl from the countryside chasing after a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country girl' looks like one phrase and is in fact the definition with the first word of the wordplay stuck to it. Erica is a standby name for setters, being Latin for heather as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Country -> AMERICA: the United States, one nation doing duty for the general word.

clue.text: Modern woman nursing broken heart? Quite the reverse, pet

indicators.note: a nurse keeps the patient in her care, so one of these pieces holds the other inside it
something broken has come apart and gone back together wrongly, so these letters change their order
the containing just described happens the other way about, and it is the piece named second that ends up inside

blocks.note: the five letters of HEART put back together in another order
Ms is the modern form of address, the one that says nothing about whether she is married

explanation.surface: A modern woman tending a broken heart, or rather the other way about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the reverse' is not an instruction to turn letters round: it swaps which piece does the holding, so the shuffled letters close over the woman. 'Pet' is the definition and also the northern English endearment the sentence signs off with.
explanation.definitionFit: pet -> HAMSTER: the cage-kept rodent is one of the standard children's pets, an example doing duty for the general word.

clue.text: Disabled and unsound

blocks.note: stressed on the first syllable, the word for somebody put out of action by illness or injury
stressed on the second syllable, said of an argument or a ticket that will not stand up

explanation.walkthrough: One spelling said two ways: IN-va-lid the person, in-VAL-id the argument. The letters never change and the stress does, which is how the setter gets a whole clue out of two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Disabled -> INVALID and unsound -> INVALID: the same seven letters name somebody laid up by illness and describe reasoning or paperwork that does not hold.

clue.text: Bloke in library performing with pained expression – not the critics' choice?

definitions.note: The definition describes a reputation rather than offering a synonym, and the question mark is the setter admitting it points at one particular performer.

indicators.note: a performing troupe moves about the stage all evening, and these letters do the same

blocks.note: a bloke is a man
anagram fodder, seven letters
ow is the noise you make when something hurts

explanation.surface: A man in the library giving a performance with a wince on his face.
explanation.walkthrough: Eighty million records sold while the reviewers sneered is the whole of the definition. He wrote jingles for State Farm and Band-Aid before Mandy made him a name.
explanation.definitionFit: not the critics' choice? -> BARRY MANILOW: the singer whose Mandy and Copacabana filled arenas for decades while the reviews stayed cold, the byword for popular but panned.
